title: Why evil (CCC 309)
hookLine: no quick answer; the whole of the faith is the answer

lines: A HOSPITAL BED. A FLOOD. A DIAGNOSIS.
NO NEAT ANSWER ON A CARD.
cards: A child in a hospital bed. A flood that takes a whole town. A friend who did everything right and got the diagnosis anyway.
And the question shows up, sometimes shouted, sometimes whispered at two in the morning: if God is good, and God made all this very good, then why?
People sometimes expect a religion to have a neat answer, one sentence on a card. The Catechism of the Catholic Church doesn't give one. It says something more honest.

teach.b: First, the honesty. Paragraph 309 asks the question straight: if God is almighty and good and cares for every creature, why does evil exist?
It says the question is as pressing as it is unavoidable, as painful as it is mysterious, and that no quick answer will do. For a book of teaching, that's a remarkable sentence.

teach.h: THE WHOLE FAITH IS THE ANSWER.
teach.b: Second, the whole faith as answer.

Instead of one line, the Catechism points to everything: the goodness of creation, the drama of human freedom and sin, God's patient love through the covenants, God becoming human in Jesus, the Spirit, the Church, the sacraments, and the promise of a life to come.
There isn't a single part of the Christian message, it says, that isn't in part an answer to evil. Not an explanation. An answer, the way a friend who shows up is an answer.
Third, good out of evil. The Catechism points to Joseph, sold as a slave by his own brothers.
Years later he tells them, in the Douay-Rheims: "You thought evil against me: but God turned it into good."
Catholics believe God doesn't cause evil, but can bring good out of it, often in ways no one could see at the time. Fourth, God in it. For Catholics, the answer runs through the cross.
Jesus doesn't explain suffering from a distance; he enters it. On the cross, Matthew says, he cries out the opening of a psalm of lament: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?"
Catholics say you're allowed to ask it too, and that you won't ask it alone.

how: Catholics bring suffering to prayer in many ways, including the psalms of lament, the Stations of the Cross, the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick, and Masses offered for those who suffer.

o: the old question of why a good God allows evil
the claim that evil isn't real, only imagined
the belief that evil is God's punishment for sin

games.q: no quick answer — tap the pairs.

s: the Catechism gives a one-sentence explanation of evil
it says no quick answer will do, and points to the whole of the faith.
Catholics believe God causes evil to teach lessons
the Church teaches God doesn't cause evil, but can bring good out of it.
on the cross, Jesus prays a psalm that asks God why
"My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" the opening of Psalm 21 (22 in most Bibles).

games.q: you're Joseph. your brothers sold you into slavery years ago. now they stand before you, afraid. what do you say?
o: you thought evil against me, but God turned it into good
games.why: Joseph forgives them and says God turned their evil into good. the Catechism uses his story to show good drawn from evil.

practice: Let one real why come up, about something that hurt you, or someone you love, or the world, and don't rush to answer it or push it away; just hold it in the open, like a stone in your hands.
If you're angry, let that be honest too; some psalms are angry. If you pray, you can bring the question to God as it is, unsolved.

wordCard.voice: Why evil. An old, hard question, which the Catechism answers not with a slogan but with the whole of the faith. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: no quick answer. When someone is suffering, showing up is an answer, and a slogan isn't. Until tomorrow.
